### 1. Data and descriptive statistics
 
# 1.1. Retrieving basic information from the v37 teaching version of the German Socio-Economic Panel (GSOEP)

```{r }
# The SOEP teaching dataset is not included in this repository.
# Set the environment variable SOEP_DATA_PATH to the local folder containing
# the v37 teaching edition before running the analysis.
soep <- Sys.getenv("SOEP_DATA_PATH")
if (soep == "") {
  stop("Please set SOEP_DATA_PATH to your local SOEP teaching-data directory.")
}
soep2 <- file.path(soep, "raw")

ppathl <- read_dta(file.path(soep, "ppathl.dta"))
cirdef <- read_dta(file.path(soep2, "cirdef.dta"))
unique(cirdef$rgroup20) #teaching data set used
```
"German data protection laws stipulate that only a maximum of 50% of all cases in the original data set may be used for teaching purposes. As of Version 35 data from 1984-2018), we provide our users with a teaching version that has the same data structure as the original data (with the exception of the EU-SILC clone) but just contains half the number of cases.The variable RGROUP20, which can be found in the data set CIRDEF, has exactly 20 values. Only cases with values from 11 to 20 may be used for teaching purposes."
https://www.diw.de/en/diw_01.c.603154.en/soep_in_the_college_classroom.html#c_diw_01.c.682607.de


**Creating panel data set for 21 years from 2000 to 2020**

ppathl = Individual Tracking File 
Person core information and respondent status for each year in long format. It contains one record for each individual and year a person has been a member of a respondent household. 
It is keyed on PID, the Cross-Wave Person Identifier, and SYEAR, the survey year identifier. 
It contains the Household ID, and never changing individual characteristics, individual weights, as well as the response status, for that individual at each wave 
https://companion.soep.de/Working%20with%20SOEP%20Data/Working%20with%20Tracking%20Data.html

```{r }
ppathl <- ppathl %>% 
  dplyr::filter(syear %in% (2000:2020)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(pid, hid, sex, gebjahr, migback, immiyear, corigin, syear, nett1, pop, 
                germborn, arefback) #select the following variables
glimpse(ppathl)
min(ppathl$syear) #year from - available in filtered data set
max(ppathl$syear) #year to - available in filtered data set
nrow(ppathl) #check number of observations to start with #467176
```

Detailed information on selected variables is available in separate excel file named documentation_variables_SOEP and in the final thesis in the Appendix table about data

**Keeping the observations with the following characteristics:**

nett1=Current survey status (old 1 digit) = 1 = Successful Interview 
pop=Sample Membership = 1 = Private HH, German HH-Head and 2= Private HH, Foreign HH-Head
```{r }
print_labels(ppathl$nett1) #see what every code means also available in documentation in English
ppathl <- ppathl %>% filter( nett1 == 1 ) #only keep successful interviews other categories are kids below survey age in the hh, not participated in the hh or missing this wave
print_labels(ppathl$pop) #see what every code means also available in documentation in English
ppathl <- ppathl %>% filter( pop == 1 | pop == 2 ) #only keep private (german and foreign) hh, not collective accommodation, institutionalized etc.
ppathl$nett1 <- NULL #remove the column, only needed for filtering
ppathl$pop <- NULL #remove the column, only needed for filtering
nrow(ppathl) #check how many observations are left #269705
```
**Retrieving information from pequiv.dta**

Generated data set, that contains large number of individual-level and household-level data to ensure a harmonized cross-country comparison
```{r }
pequiv <- read_dta(file.path(soep, "pequiv.dta")) #cca 3-4 minutes loading
pequiv <- pequiv%>% 
  dplyr::filter(syear %in% (2000:2020)) %>%
  dplyr::select(pid=pid, syear=syear, age=d11101, mar=d11104, hhsize=d11106, hhinc=i11102,
                edu=d11109, ls=p11101, empl=e11102)
nrow(pequiv) #399279
```

The observations in both data frames, ppathl and pequiv, are identified by the variable pid and syear
```{r }
head(pequiv)
head(ppathl)
```

**Joining information from both data frames ppathl and pequiv**

The function left_join() keeps all observations in the data frame ppathl
```{r }
d <- left_join(ppathl, pequiv, by=c("pid", "syear")) #keeps all observations in x in this case in ppathl this is the main tracking file
glimpse(d)
nrow(d) #all observations kept from ppathl #269,705
rm(ppathl, pequiv, cirdef) #remove original data files
length(unique(d$pid)) #44978
length(unique(d$hid)) #24916
d %>%  filter(syear == 2020) %>%summarise(unique_count = n_distinct(pid)) %>%  print() #15159 pids in 2020
d %>%  filter(syear == 2020) %>%summarise(unique_count = n_distinct(hid)) %>%  print() #9748 hids in 2020 
```

The data set includes all necessary variables for the analysis

```{r }
contents(d)
# View(d)  # optional interactive inspection
```

# 1.2. Re code negative numbers as missing values

Missing values in the SOEP are recorded as negative numbers
R uses NA to indicate missing values. Therefore, it is needed SOEP missing values to be recoded to R missing values

**Re code missing values:**

```{r }
colnames(d)

#pid
table(d$pid[d$pid<0]) #check negative values, no negative

#hid
table(d$hid[d$hid<0]) #check negative values, no negative  
```

```{r }
#sex
table(d$sex[d$sex<0]) #check negative values, -3 = [en] Answer improbable, 8 obs with missing values
d$sex[d$sex<0] <- NA #transform to R n/a value
d %>%filter(is.na(sex))%>%group_by(migback)%>%summarise(count_nas = n())%>%arrange(desc(count_nas))
#applies to natives
d %>%filter(is.na(sex))%>%group_by(syear)%>%summarise(count_nas = n())%>%arrange(desc(count_nas))
#missing values only in the last two years, 2019 and 2020
d %>% filter(is.na(sex)) #4 pids in 2 consecutive years did not provide an answer, item non-response,
#assumed missing at random
```

```{r }
#gebjahr
table(d$gebjahr[d$gebjahr<0]) #check negative values, -1 =	[-1] No Answer, 3 obs with missing values
d$gebjahr[d$gebjahr<0] <- NA #transform to R n/a value
d %>% filter(is.na(gebjahr)) #more questions are not answered, partial non response but not completely unit non response
#assumed missing at random
```

```{r }
#migback 
table(d$migback[d$migback<0]) #check negative values, no negative 
```

```{r }
#immiyear
table(d$immiyear[d$immiyear<0]) #check negative values, -1 = No Answer, 2289 obs; -2 = Does not apply, 222873 obs
immiyearcheck <- d %>% filter(immiyear == -2) #natives and second gen immigrants should be not apply
unique(immiyearcheck$migback) #only migback 1 and 3 
immiyearcheck %>%  group_by(migback, immiyear ) %>%  summarise(Count = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = immiyear, values_from = Count, values_fill = list(Count = 0))
#it is confirmed natives and second generation have no immigration year

#answer -2 (Does not apply) will be recoded to zero as it is not considered a missing value
d <- d %>%
  mutate(across(c(immiyear), ~case_when(
    .x == -1 ~ NA,
    .x == -2 ~ 0,
    TRUE ~ .x  )))  

#check if correctly recoded 
d %>% group_by(migback) %>% dplyr::summarize(count_na = sum(is.na(immiyear)), .groups = "drop") %>% print(n = 21)
#missing values only in immigrants, 2289 observations

d %>%filter(is.na(immiyear))%>%group_by(syear)%>%summarise(count_nas = n())%>%arrange(desc(count_nas))
#2289 obs have missing immigration year and it appears missing in every survey year, mostly in year 2000 and next in 2020, assumed missing at random 

#filter and group by pid
d %>%filter(is.na(immiyear))%>%group_by(pid)%>%summarise(count_nas = n())%>%arrange(desc(count_nas))  
#order by count_nas in descending order
#669 pids have missing immigration year, some in every survey since the beginning of the sample
rm(immiyearcheck)
```

```{r }
d$corigin[d$corigin<0] <- NA #transform to R n/a value
```

# 1.3. Selecting a subset of observations

**Only selecting natives and first generation immigrants, 1 and 2**

```{r }
#Check the information in migback and germborn as they are connected for correct filtering of immigrants and natives 
table(d$migback) #1	= [en] no migration background; 2 = [en] direct migration background; 
#3 = [en] indirect migration background #1 (209540)      #2 (46832)    #3 (13333)
table(d$germborn) #1 = [en] born in Germany or immigr.<1950 and 2 = [en] not born in Germany
#1 (222873) #2 (46832)
d%>%group_by(germborn,migback)%>% summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop')
#It is confirmed that individuals born in Germany are with migration background 1 (209540) and 3 (13333) total 222873 germborn with value 1.
#so migration background value 2 (46832) is immigrants not born in Germany, with direct migration background
d%>%filter(germborn==1)%>%  pull(corigin) %>% unique() %>%print() #all are born in Germany
#Only migback 1 and 2 will be selected for further analysis, 1 representing natives and 2 immigrants
d <- d %>%
  filter(migback %in% c(1, 2))
nrow(d) #256372 obs left
d$germborn <- NULL #this variable is now equal to migback
```

**Only selecting ages from 25 to 65, working population**

```{r }
min(d$age, na.rm = TRUE) #12 years
max(d$age, na.rm = TRUE) #102 years

#Check how many immigrants and natives are in these two groups
d %>%filter(age < 25) %>%summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') #26179 obs/256372 = 10% whole sample
d %>%filter(age > 65) %>%summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') #46411 obs/256372 = 18% whole sample
d %>%filter(migback==2 & age < 25) %>%summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') #4692 obs only immigrants
d %>%filter(migback==2 & age > 65) %>%summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') #4038 obs only immigrants
d %>%filter(migback==1 & age < 25) %>%summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') #21487 obs natives
d %>%filter(migback==1 & age > 65) %>%summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop') #42373 obs natives

#Check age distribution 
count_age <- d %>% group_by(age) %>%  summarise(count = n(), .groups = 'drop')
ggplot(count_age, aes(x = age, y = count)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distribution by Age",
       x = "Age",
       y = "Count")

#Filter the ages
d <- d%>%
  filter(is.na(age) | 
    age >= 25 & age <= 65)
nrow(d) #183782 obs left
rm(count_age)
```

**Individuals in the top and bottom 0.5% of the income distribution are excluded from the analysis**

```{r }
d <- d %>% filter(is.na(hhinc) | 
  hhinc > quantile(hhinc, probs = 0.005, na.rm = TRUE) &
    hhinc < quantile(hhinc, probs = 0.995, na.rm = TRUE))
nrow(d) #181969 obs left
```
# 1.4. Further cleaning of missing values and transforming variables for analysis

**Count and percentage of NA values in each column after subseting the data**

```{r }
na_count_per_column <- colSums(is.na(d))
print(na_count_per_column) #education, hh income and life satisfaction are top 3 with missing values
sum(na_count_per_column) #10142 missing values across observations
gg_miss_var(d) #Plot the number of missing for each variable, education, hh income, ls and immigration year
```

**Plot the percentage of missing values for each variable**

```{r }
missing_percentages <- d%>%
  dplyr::summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))/n() * 100)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Column", values_to = "PercentageMissing")
print(missing_percentages)

ggplot(missing_percentages, aes(x = Column, y = PercentageMissing, fill = Column)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Percentage of Missing Values by Column",
       x = "Column",
       y = "Percentage Missing") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) # Rotate x-axis labels for readability
rm(missing_percentages)

#Combinations of missingness across cases
gg_miss_upset(d) #most combo is education and hh income
```

**Drop observations with missing values on key variables** 

Missing values cannot be used in the analysis. 
The analysis is based on a data set with complete cases only.
So all observations with missing values on any variable are removed.
That is, missing values in any variable are excluded and only complete cases are used.
```{r }
nrow(d) #181969 observations
d1 <-d #to compare before and after missing values difference
d <- na.omit(d)
nrow(d) #172675 observations are kept
nrow(d1)-nrow(d) #9294 are deleted, still considerable amount of data to be analysed
(nrow(d)-nrow(d1))/nrow(d1)*100 #5% decrease in observations
colSums(is.na(d)) #no missing values across data set
```

**Creating a dummy variable for male**

```{r }
d %>%  mutate(sex = as_factor(sex))%>% group_by(sex) %>% summarise(count = n()) #80810 male and 91865 female
d$male <- ifelse( d$sex == 1, yes = 1, no = 0 )
label(d$male) <- "Male (0/1)"
d$male <- factor(d$male,levels = c(0,1),labels = c("Female", "Male"))
table(d$male) #80810 male and 91865 female but some will be deleted by ysm later not final number
```
**Creating a dummy variable for immigrants**

```{r }
d %>%  mutate(migback = as_factor(migback))%>% group_by(migback) %>% summarise(count = n()) #140778 natives and 31897 immigrants
d$immigrants <- ifelse( d$migback == 2, yes = 1, no = 0)
label(d$immigrants) <- "Immigrants (0/1)"
d$immigrants <- factor(d$immigrants, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Natives", "Immigrants"))
table(d$immigrants) #140778 natives and 31897 immigrants but some will be deleted by ysm later not final number
```

**Creating a dummy variable for marital status**

```{r }
d %>%  mutate(mar = as_factor(mar))%>% group_by(mar) %>% summarise(count = n()) #116983 married rest not married
d$mar <- ifelse( d$mar == 1, yes = 1, no = 0 )
label(d$mar) <- "Marital status (0/1)"
d$mar <- factor(d$mar,levels = c(0,1),labels = c("Not married", "Married"))
table(d$mar) #55692 not married and 116983 married but some will be deleted by ysm later not final number
```

**Creating a dummy variable for employment status**

```{r }
d %>%  mutate(empl = as_factor(empl))%>% group_by(empl) %>% summarise(count = n()) #37424 not employed and 135251 employed
d$empl <- ifelse( d$empl == 1, yes = 1, no = 0 )
label(d$empl) <- "Employment status (0/1)"
d$empl <- factor(d$empl,levels = c(0,1),labels = c("Not employed", "Employed"))
table(d$empl) #37424 not employed and 135251 employed but some will be deleted by ysm later not final number
```

**Creating a variable for equivalised income based on formula hhinc/sqrt(hhsize) in log**

```{r }
d$inc <-d$hhinc/sqrt(d$hhsize)
d$log_inc <-log(d$inc)
```

### 2. Estimation

## 2.1. Pooled OLS with cluster robust standard errors per pid

# 2.1.1. Pooled OLS without controls

```{r }
colnames(d_panel)
plm_model_1 <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel,  model = "pooling")
summary(plm_model_1)

ols_model_1 <- lm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel)
summary(ols_model_1)

#Test for heteroscedasticity
bptest(ols_model_1) #small p-value, heteroscedasticity present use cluster-robust SE per pid

#Compute clustered standard errors
clustered_se_1 <- vcovHC(plm_model_1, type = "HC1", cluster = "group") #type = "HC1"
clustered_se_1.1 <-sqrt(diag(clustered_se_1))

#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
coeftest(plm_model_1, vcov = clustered_se_1)
```

# 2.1.2 Pooled OLS with controls, adding gender and marital status

```{r }
plm_model_2 <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status),
                   data = d_panel,  model = "pooling")
summary(plm_model_2)

ols_model_2 <-lm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status),
                   data = d_panel)
summary(ols_model_2)

#Test for heteroscedasticity
bptest(ols_model_2) #small p-value, heteroscedasticity present use cluster-robust SE per pid

#Compute clustered standard errors
clustered_se_2 <- vcovHC(plm_model_2, type = "HC1", cluster = "group") #type = "HC1"
clustered_se_2.1 <-sqrt(diag(clustered_se_2))


#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
coeftest(plm_model_2, vcov = clustered_se_2)
```

```{r }
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income, data = d_panel,  model = "pooling")

summary(plm_model_3)

                     Education+Log_Income, data = d_panel)

clustered_se_3.1 <-sqrt(diag(clustered_se_3))
```

# 2.1.4. Pooled OLS with controls, adding employment status

```{r }
plm_model_4 <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income+as.factor(Employment_status),
                   data = d_panel,  model = "pooling")

                    as.factor(Migration_background)+as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income+as.factor(Employment_status), data = d_panel)
summary(ols_model_4)

#Test for heteroscedasticity

clustered_se_4.1 <-sqrt(diag(clustered_se_4))

```

## 2.2. Model comparison

# 2.2.1. Likelihood ratio test for nested models and F - tests (same results)

```{r }
#Likelihood ratio test for nested models
lrtest(ols_model_1, ols_model_2)
#rejects the restricted model small p value, suggesting that Model 2, with more parameters, provides a significantly better fit to the data than Model 1
lrtest(ols_model_2, ols_model_3) 
#rejects the restricted model small p value, suggesting that Model 3, with more parameters, provides a significantly better fit to the data than Model 2
lrtest(ols_model_3, ols_model_4)
#rejects the restricted model small p value, suggesting that Model 4, with more parameters, provides a significantly better fit to the data than Model 3

#Multiple Linear Restrictions F test
myH0_2 <- c("as.factor(Gender)1  ","as.factor(Marital_status)1")
linearHypothesis(ols_model_2, myH0_2, vcov=vcovHC(ols_model_2, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")) 
#rejects the restricted model small p value, suggesting that Model 2, with more parameters, provides a significantly better fit to the data than Model 1

myH0_3 <- c("Education", "Log_Income")
linearHypothesis(ols_model_3, myH0_3, vcov=vcovHC(ols_model_3,type="HC1", cluster = "group"))
#rejects the restricted model small p value, suggesting that Model 3, with more parameters, provides a significantly better fit to the data than Model 2

myH0_4 <- c("as.factor(Employment_status)1")
linearHypothesis(ols_model_4, myH0_4, vcov=vcovHC(ols_model_4,type="HC1", cluster = "group"))
#rejects the restricted model small p value, suggesting that Model 4, with more parameters, provides a significantly better fit to the data than Model 3

```

# 2.2.2. Model comparison using information criteria

```{r }
#Lower AIC and BIC values and higher adjusted R-squared values suggest a better model fit.
#Akaike information criterion (AIC):
AIC(ols_model_1, ols_model_2) #model 2 has better fit, lower AIC
AIC(ols_model_2, ols_model_3) #model 3 has better fit, lower AIC
AIC(ols_model_3, ols_model_4) #model 4 has better fit, lower AIC

#Bayes information criterion (BIC):
BIC(ols_model_1, ols_model_2) #model 2 has better fit, lower BIC
BIC(ols_model_2, ols_model_3) #model 3 has better fit, lower BIC
BIC(ols_model_3, ols_model_4) #model 4 has better fit, lower BIC

#The AIC for a simple Pooled OLS model and a Pooled OLS model with cluster-robust standard errors would be the same because the calculation of AIC is based on the model fit (likelihood) and does not consider the computation or adjustment of standard errors. The choice to use cluster-robust standard errors affects inference testing hypotheses about parameters, constructing confidence intervals) but not the estimation of the model parameters themselves or the model's likelihood.
```

## 2.4. Random effects estimator (FGLS)

# 2.4.1. Random effects estimator (FGLS) without controls

```{r }
re_1 <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel, model = "random")
summary(re_1)

#Test for heteroscedasticity
bptest(re_1) #small p-value, heteroscedasticity present use cluster-robust SE per pid

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_1 <- vcovHC(re_1, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_1.1 <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_1))

#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_1)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_1 <- coef(re_1) 
coeftest(re_1, vcov = robust_se_1)
```

# 2.4.3. Random effects estimator (FGLS) with controls, adding education and log income

```{r }
re_3 <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income, data = d_panel, model = "random")
summary(re_3)

#Test for heteroscedasticity
bptest(re_3) #small p-value, heteroscedasticity present use cluster-robust SE per pid

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_3 <- vcovHC(re_3, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_3.1 <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_3))

#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_3)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_3 <- coef(re_3) 
coeftest(re_3, vcov = robust_se_3)
```

# 2.5.1 Testing for random effects: Breusch-Pagan Lagrange multiplier (LM)
Test of individual and/or time effects for panel models.
```{r }
#Breusch-Pagan Lagrange Multiplier for random effects. Null is no panel effect (i.e. OLS better)
#Model 1
plmtest(plm_model_1, type=c("bp"))
#p-value < 0.00000000000000022, reject the null H, proceed with RE model, POLS is not appropriate
#Model 2
plmtest(plm_model_2, type=c("bp"))
#p-value < 0.00000000000000022, reject the null H, proceed with RE model, POLS is not appropriate
#Model 3
plmtest(plm_model_3, type=c("bp"))
#p-value < 0.00000000000000022, reject the null H, proceed with RE model, POLS is not appropriate
#Model 4
plmtest(plm_model_4, type=c("bp"))
#p-value < 0.00000000000000022, reject the null H, proceed with RE model, POLS is not appropriate

#The LM test helps you decide between a random effects regression and a simple OLS regression. The null hypothesis in the LM test is that variances across entities is zero. This is, no  significant difference across units (i.e. no panel effect).
```

```{r }
#Solving the quadratic equation
#RE model 1
a_1 <-coef_re_1[5]/100
b_1 <-coef_re_1[4]
c_1 <-coef_re_1[6]
quad <- function(a, b, c)
{
  a <- as.complex(a)
  answer <- c((-b + sqrt(b^2 - 4 * a * c)) / (2 * a),
              (-b - sqrt(b^2 - 4 * a * c)) / (2 * a))
  if(all(Im(answer) == 0)) answer <- Re(answer)
  if(answer[1] == answer[2]) return(answer[1])
  answer
}
```

```{r }
                    as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel, model = "within")
summary(fe_1)
```

## 2.7.6 Hausman test FE vs. RE

```{r }
#Robust SE Hausman test Model 1
diff_coefs_1 <- coef_fe_1 - coef_re_1[2:5]
robust_se_1_del<- robust_se_1[, c("Age", "I((Age^2)/100)", "YSM", "I((YSM^2)/100)" )]
robust_se_1_del<- robust_se_1_del[c("Age", "I((Age^2)/100)", "YSM", "I((YSM^2)/100)"),]
diff_var_1 <- robust_se_fe_1 - robust_se_1_del

#Calculate t statistics and p-value
H_1 <- t(diff_coefs_1) %*% solve(diff_var_1) %*% diff_coefs_1
H_1
df_1 <- length(diff_coefs_1) # Adjust this based on the specific comparison
df_1
p_value_1 <- pchisq(H_1, df_1, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_value_1 #0.069393 very weak evidence to not reject the the null hypothesis of the Hausman test, random effects model appears to be an appropriate choice at 5% level


#Robust SE Hausman test Model 2
coef_re_2_del <- coef_re_2[-(1)]
coef_re_2_del <- coef_re_2_del[-(5:6)]
diff_coefs_2 <- coef_fe_2 - coef_re_2_del
robust_se_2_del<- robust_se_2[, c("Age", "I((Age^2)/100)", "YSM", "I((YSM^2)/100)", "as.factor(Marital_status)1" )]
robust_se_2_del<- robust_se_2_del[c("Age", "I((Age^2)/100)", "YSM", "I((YSM^2)/100)", "as.factor(Marital_status)1"), ]
diff_var_2 <- robust_se_fe_2 - robust_se_2_del

#Calculate t statistics and p-value
H_2 <- t(diff_coefs_2) %*% solve(diff_var_2) %*% diff_coefs_2
H_2
df_2 <- length(diff_coefs_2) # Adjust this based on the specific comparison
df_2
p_value_2 <- pchisq(H_2, df_2, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_value_2 #0.0000000000000667829 very small p value reject the null, FE is the appropriate choice.


#Robust SE Hausman test Model 3
```

### 3. Prediction for OLS and RE models

## 3.1. Prediction for all OLS models

# 3.1.1. Predicted LS per age without controls - OLS model 1

**Create the table**
```{r }
# Create a data frame for natives
natives_df_1 <- data.frame(
  Age = 25:65,
  YSM = rep(0, 41),
  Migration_background = rep(0, 41))

# Create a data frame for immigrants
immigrants_df_1 <- data.frame(
  Age = 25:65,
  YSM = 1:41,
  Migration_background = rep(1, 41))

# Combine the two data frames
combined_df_1 <- rbind(natives_df_1, immigrants_df_1)
```

**Predict the LS for the model OLS_1 without controls**
```{r }
combined_df_1$p_pred_ols <- predict(ols_model_1, newdata = combined_df_1,
                              type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)

combined_df_1$p_pred_plm <- predict(plm_model_1, newdata = combined_df_1,
                              type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)

combined_df_1$diff_pred <-combined_df_1$p_pred_ols-combined_df_1$p_pred_plm
```

**Plot the prediction for the model OLS_1 without controls**
```{r }
#Plot the prediction OLS_1 model

#Plotting Predictions Against Age for Natives and Immigrants
p1_ols <- ggplot(combined_df_1, aes(x = Age, y = p_pred_ols, linetype = factor(Migration_background))) +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 1) +  # Set color to black and adjust line size as needed
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"), labels = c('Natives', 'Immigrants')) +  # Define linetypes
```

### 4. Gender analysis

**Split the data into male and female**
```{r }
d_panel_f <- d_panel %>% filter(Gender==0) #females 91231 same as DS
d_panel_m <- d_panel %>% filter(Gender==1) #males 79981 same as DS
```

## 4.1. Female estimation
```{r data}
#Estimate model 1 no controls
re_1_f <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel_f, model = "random")
summary(re_1_f)

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_1_f <- vcovHC(re_1_f, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_1.1_f <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_1_f))

#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_1_f)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_1_f <- coef(re_1_f) 
coeftest(re_1_f, vcov = robust_se_1_f)

#Estimate model 4 with full set of controls
re_4_f <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income+as.factor(Employment_status),
                   data = d_panel_f, model = "random")
summary(re_4_f)

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_4_f <- vcovHC(re_4_f, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_4.1_f <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_4_f))

#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_4_f)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_4_f <- coef(re_4_f) 
coeftest(re_4_f, vcov = robust_se_4_f)
```

## 4.2. Male estimation
```{r }
#Estimate model 1 no controls
re_1_m <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel_m, model = "random")
summary(re_1_m)

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_1_m <- vcovHC(re_1_m, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_1.1_m <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_1_m))


#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_1_m)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_1_m <- coef(re_1_m) 
coeftest(re_1_m, vcov = robust_se_1_m)

#Estimate model 4 with full set of controls
re_4_m <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income+as.factor(Employment_status),
                   data = d_panel_m, model = "random")
summary(re_4_m)

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_4_m <- vcovHC(re_4_m, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_4.1_m <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_4_m))

#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_4_m)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_4_m <- coef(re_4_m) 
coeftest(re_4_m, vcov = robust_se_4_m)
```

## 4.2. Print the results for both genders and both models
```{r }
stargazer(re_1_f, re_4_f, re_1_m, re_4_m, type="text", 
          title = "Random Effects Results",
          se = list(robust_se_1.1_f, robust_se_4.1_f, robust_se_1.1_m, robust_se_4.1_m),
          covariate.labels = c("Age", "Age (squared/100)", "YSM", "YSM (squared/100)", 
                               "Immigrants", "Married",
                               "Education", "Income (log)", "Employed"),
          dep.var.labels="Life satisfaction", column.labels =c("Female M1", "Female M4", 
                                                               "Male M1", "Male M4"),
          out = "models_re_gender.html")
```

## 4.3. Interpretation of the coefficients RE models - gender analysis

**Interpretation for females**
```{r }
#RE model 1
coef_re_1_f
#RE model 4
coef_re_4_f
#Age
#RE model 1

min_age_1_f #55.26765 
#RE model 4

min_age_4_f #51.36657 

#YSM
# Solving the quadratic equation
#RE model 1
a_1_f <-coef_re_1_f[5]/100
b_1_f<-coef_re_1_f[4]
c_1_f<-coef_re_1_f[6]

ysm_1_f <- quad(a = a_1_f, b = b_1_f, c = c_1_f)
ysm_1_f #25.096467  
age_parity_1_f<-ysm_1_f+25 #25 start of immigration year 1
age_parity_1_f #50.09647  

#RE model 4

age_parity_4_f #54.00358
```

### 5. Country of origin analysis

**Split the data per country of origin**
```{r }
colnames(d_panel)
unique(d_panel$Country_group) #"Germany" ,"Eastern Europe", "Balkans", 
#"Western Europe & Offshoots","Rest of the World" 
d_panel_ee <- d_panel %>% filter(Country_group=="Germany" | Country_group=="Eastern Europe")
#140778+12630 =153408 same as DS
d_panel_we <- d_panel %>% filter(Country_group=="Germany" | Country_group=="Western Europe & Offshoots") 
#140778+4100 =144878 same as DS
d_panel_b <- d_panel %>% filter(Country_group=="Germany" | Country_group=="Balkans")
#140778+6954 =147732 same as DS
d_panel_r <- d_panel %>% filter(Country_group=="Germany" | Country_group=="Rest of the World")
#140778+6750 =147528 same as DS
```

## 5.1. Eastern Europe estimation
```{r }
#Estimate model 1 no controls
re_1_ee <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel_ee, model = "random")
summary(re_1_ee)

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_1_ee <- vcovHC(re_1_ee, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_1.1_ee <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_1_ee))


#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_1_ee)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_1_ee <- coef(re_1_ee) 
coeftest(re_1_ee, vcov = robust_se_1_ee)

#Estimate model 4 with full set of controls
re_4_ee <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)++as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income+as.factor(Employment_status),
                   data = d_panel_ee, model = "random")
summary(re_4_ee)

#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_4_ee <- vcovHC(re_4_ee, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_4.1_ee <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_4_ee))

#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
#round(summary(re_4_ee)$coefficients, 4)
coef_re_4_ee <- coef(re_4_ee) 
coeftest(re_4_ee, vcov = robust_se_4_ee)
```

## 5.5. Print the results for all models and all countries
```{r }
#Model 1
stargazer(re_1_ee, re_1_we, re_1_b, re_1_r, type="text", 
          title = "Random Effects Results Model 1",
          se = list(robust_se_1.1_ee, robust_se_1.1_we, robust_se_1.1_b, robust_se_1.1_r),
          covariate.labels = c("Age", "Age (squared/100)", "YSM", "YSM (squared/100)", 
                               "Immigrants"),
          dep.var.labels="Life satisfaction", column.labels =c("EE", "WE", 
                                                               "Balkans", "Rest"),
          out = "models_re_cor_1.html")

#Model 4
stargazer(re_4_ee, re_4_we, re_4_b, re_4_r, type="text", 
          title = "Random Effects Results Model 4",
          se = list(robust_se_4.1_ee, robust_se_4.1_we, robust_se_4.1_b, robust_se_4.1_r),
          covariate.labels = c("Age", "Age (squared/100)", "YSM", "YSM (squared/100)", 
                               "Immigrants", "Male", "Married",
                               "Education", "Income (log)", "Employed"),
          dep.var.labels="Life satisfaction", column.labels =c("EE", "WE", 
                                                               "Balkans", "Rest"),
          out = "models_re_cor_4.html")
```

### 6. Attrition calculate loss of data
```{r }
#Testing with balanced panel and exploring differences
d_panel_bal <- make.pbalanced(d_panel, balance.type = "shared.individuals")
#Check dimensions and balance of the panel data
pdim(d_panel_bal)
#number of individuals = 725, number of years = 21, number of total observations = 15225
#Compare loss of data
pdim(d_panel)
#Unbalanced Panel: n = 28829, T = 1-21, N = 171212
#(171212-15225)/171212*100=91.10752% decrease in observations

#Estimation with balanced sample
#Model 1
re_1_bal <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background), data = d_panel_bal, model = "random")
summary(re_1_bal)
#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_1_bal <- vcovHC(re_1_bal, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_1.1_bal <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_1_bal))
#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
coef_re_1_bal <- coef(re_1_bal) 
coeftest(re_1_bal, vcov = robust_se_1_bal)

#Model 4
re_4_bal <- plm(Life_satisfaction ~ 1+Age+I((Age^2)/100)+YSM+I((YSM^2)/100)+
                    as.factor(Migration_background)+as.factor(Gender)+ as.factor(Marital_status)+
                     Education+Log_Income+as.factor(Employment_status),
                   data = d_panel_bal, model = "random")
summary(re_4_bal)
#Compute clustered standard errors
robust_se_4_bal <- vcovHC(re_4_bal, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
robust_se_4.1_bal <-sqrt(diag(robust_se_4_bal))
#Display coefficients with clustered standard errors
coef_re_4_bal <- coef(re_4_bal) 
coeftest(re_4_bal, vcov = robust_se_4_bal)

#Print the results
stargazer(re_1, re_1_bal, re_4, re_4_bal, type="text", 
          title = "Random Effects Results",
          se = list(robust_se_1.1, robust_se_1.1_bal, robust_se_4.1, robust_se_4.1_bal),
          covariate.labels = c("Age", "Age (squared/100)", "YSM", "YSM (squared/100)", 
                               "Immigrants", "Male", "Married",
                               "Education", "Income (log)", "Employed"),
          dep.var.labels="Life satisfaction", column.labels =c("M1 Unbalanced", "M1 Balanced", 
                                                               "M4 Unbalanced", "M4 Balanced"),
          out = "models_re_bal.html")

#Predict the LS
combined_df_1$p_pred_re_bal <- predict(re_1_bal, newdata = combined_df_1,
                              type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)
combined_df_4$p_pred_re_bal <- predict(re_4_bal, newdata = combined_df_4,
                              type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)

#Plot the predictions Model 1
#Plotting Predictions Against Age for Natives and Immigrants
ggplot(combined_df_1, aes(x = Age, y = p_pred_re_bal, linetype = factor(Migration_background))) +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 1) +  # Set color to black and adjust line size as needed
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"), labels = c('Natives', 'Immigrants')) +  # Define linetypes
  labs(#title = "Predicted Life Satisfaction Across Age for Natives and Immigrants",
       x = "Age", y = "Predicted Life Satisfaction",
       linetype = "Group") +  # Update legend title for linetype
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(25, 65), breaks = seq(25, 65, 5))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(6, 8), breaks = seq(6, 8, 0.5))

#Plot the predictions Model 4
#Plotting Predictions Against Age for Natives and Immigrants
ggplot(combined_df_4, aes(x = Age, y = p_pred_re_bal, linetype = factor(Migration_background))) +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 1) +  # Set color to black and adjust line size as needed
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"), labels = c('Natives', 'Immigrants')) +  # Define linetypes
  labs(#title = "Predicted Life Satisfaction Across Age for Natives and Immigrants",
       x = "Age", y = "Predicted Life Satisfaction",
       linetype = "Group") +  # Update legend title for linetype
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(25, 65), breaks = seq(25, 65, 5))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(6, 8), breaks = seq(6, 8, 0.5))
```

```{r }
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.4,  0.9), breaks = seq(-0.4, 0.9, 0.1))
min(reshape_4$diff_nat_imm_b)
max(reshape_4$diff_nat_imm_b)
p_ysm_4_b

#Plot model 4 Rest
p_ysm_4_r <-ggplot(reshape_4, aes(x = YSM.1, y = diff_nat_imm_r)) +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 1, linetype = "dashed") +  # Set color to black and adjust line size as needed
  labs(#title = "Difference in LS of immigrants relative to natives of same age",
       x = "YSM", y = "Diff in LS of immigrants to natives")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", color = "gray", size = 1)+
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 41), breaks = seq(1, 40, 3))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.4,  0.9), breaks = seq(-0.4, 0.9, 0.1))
min(reshape_4$diff_nat_imm_r)
max(reshape_4$diff_nat_imm_r)
p_ysm_4_r

#Combine all YSM plots 
combined_plot_ysm_cor_4 <- (p_ysm_4_ee + ggtitle("YSM RE Model 4 East Europe")) + 
                        (p_ysm_4_we + ggtitle("YSM RE Model 4 West Europe")) + 
                        (p_ysm_4_b + ggtitle("YSM RE Model 4 Balkans")) + 
                        (p_ysm_4_r + ggtitle("YSM RE Model 4 Rest")) + 
plot_layout(nrow = 2, guides = 'collect') # This collects and displays the guides (legends) only once


combined_plot_ysm_cor_4 #run it in the console
#ggsave("combined_plot_ysm_cor_4.pdf", combined_plot_ysm_cor_4)
```
